k-1.x_notes: Strengths: seven concrete fill-the-board problems, all boards at actual size (1-inch triangles). It builds well from an easy entry (which single colors fill a hexagon) to the hexagon piece combinations (8 to 10 multisets, 12 drawing hexagons). Problem 4 (fewest greens, with a side-5 prediction) and Problem 5 (which shapes blue can fill, including a 6-triangle shape with 4 up and 2 down) carry the coloring kernel. Problem 6 is a good fewest-pieces puzzle (three trapezoids fill the side-3 triangle), and Problem 7 asks children to invent a shape blue cannot fill. The mathematics is correct. Weaknesses: a Name field on every page, no week or activity title in the header, and only a page number in the footer. No shared rule about staying on the lines. Problem 3 (count the greens in triangles whose grid is already drawn) is fairly routine counting. The definition of 'same way' in Problem 2 is abstract for kindergartners.
k-1.y_notes: Strengths: the header, footer and one-line shared rule follow the organizer's format, and there are no Name fields. Small block icons inline help pre-readers. Six varied, concrete problems: cover with blue or X it, including an 8-triangle trapezoid (5 up, 3 down) with even area that cannot be covered; fewest greens on side-2, 3 and 4 triangles; all blue tilings of the small hexagon (2) and the elongated hexagon (3), giving K-1 an entry to kernel 2; fewest blocks of any kind on three boards (minimums 3, 3 and 4, all checked). Problem 5 is a two-player placing game with correct answers (first, second, first, first, second) that is engaging and can be replayed for a long time. It finishes with finding all 6 tilings of the 1-2-2 hexagon on an actual-size board, with small copies to draw on. Weaknesses: 'be sure to win' needs adult support at this age. Problem 3 gives one more shape than there are tilings, which may make children hunt for one that does not exist (defensible). Placed blocks leave no record in Problem 3.
k-1.reason: Both are concrete and correct, but Y gives K-1 more real mathematics and variety: a strategy game, both kernels, and finding all tilings. It also follows the page format. X spends a page on routine counting and puts Name fields on every page.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Strengths: a rich, well-chosen sequence of boards, all at actual size and all checked. A star (tileable), two trapezoids with even area but unbalanced counts (7/5 and 7/9), an irregular balanced board D (tileable), an odd board E (15), holes F (one up, one down: tileable) and G (two downs: not), and the hexagon hole-pair rule H (every up-down pair works, checked). Board J is balanced 7/7 yet cannot be covered, showing that the count is necessary but not sufficient. Fewest greens on triangles of side 3 to 6 gives plenty of building, then the side 10/100 generalization with 'how do you know'. Chevrons on side 4 and 5 (4 and 5 left uncovered, the same as blue, checked). Problem 8 asks whether a board exists that purple can cover and blue cannot, or the reverse, with a grid. Weaknesses: Name fields and a nonstandard header and footer. Problems 6 and 7 are crowded onto the last page with no workspace. Problem 3 has only one board and nowhere to record the hole pairs tried. Problem 7 refers to 'the big triangle with sides 4' without pointing to the page.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Strengths: the header, footer and shared rule are in the correct format. Similar contrasting boards, all correct: star yes, side-3 triangle (odd), trapezoid with even area but unbalanced, elongated hexagon yes. Holes: two ups (no), a bowtie that is balanced 4/4 but joined only at a point (no, a nice subtle case), up plus down (yes). Fewest greens on side 2 to 5 with a lower-bound explanation, and 10/100. A chevron table for sides 2 to 5 lets children compare the data directly (purple 4, 5, 4, 5 against blue 2, 3, 4, 5, checked). Problem 6 is a good inverse design task (a connected 20-triangle board needing at least 6 greens; solvable). The hexagon two-green rule problem has 10 small hexagons for recording trials. Weaknesses: 'explain why' is appended to most problems, with many writing lines. The biggest triangle is side 5, so there is somewhat less building than in X. There is no balanced, connected board that cannot be covered (like X's J).
grades-2-3.reason: The mathematics and the sequence are nearly identical and both are sound. Y's format, recording space for the hole-rule search, and the design task give it a slight edge over X's somewhat richer set of boards (board J and the purple-versus-blue question).

grades-4-5.x_notes: Strengths: a full kernel-2 sequence on actual-size boards. Count the 1-2-2 hexagon (6), draw the flip graph as dots and lines in a provided box, define ribbons and ask which L/R strings occur and whether a ribbon determines the covering (a bijection to C(4,2)). It then generalizes to board B (1-2-3, 10) and the 1-4-4 hexagon (70). Board C (2-2-2, 20) comes with 25 copies, followed by one shortest-flip puzzle, the farthest pair (8), and parity of round trips for A and C. A cube-stack picture (checked as a valid covering) asks what a flip does and how many cubes the box holds. Weaknesses: Name fields and a nonstandard header and footer. It never asks what a flip does to a ribbon, the key fact in the kernel. The parity question (Problem 8) comes before the cube view that would explain it. Problems 6 to 9 are crammed on one page with little workspace. Only one concrete flip-route puzzle.
grades-4-5.y_notes: Strengths: correct format with a shared rule. Count the 1-2-2 hexagon with an explanation (10 small boards), then the flip definition and the graph. Three concrete shortest-flip puzzles on an actual-size side-2 hexagon board; the coverings are drawn validly (checked). A round-trip task (find a 4-flip loop that does not repeat a hexagon; can you do it in 5 or 7?) builds the parity discovery by hand before ribbons are introduced. Ribbons generalize to two ribbons on the hexagon, and the problem asks exactly what a flip does to them (it swaps an adjacent LR pair). Then comes a proof of parity and of the lower bound from E to F, a count of the 20 coverings of the side-2 hexagon, and a count of the 1-3-3 hexagon (20). The order is good: act, then discover, then prove. Weaknesses: Problem 2 makes children redraw all coverings on a fixed grid to connect them (clumsy). A full page of writing lines for the proof. No cube-stack interpretation and a less ambitious generalization than X's 70.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are mathematically strong and correct. Y is more hands-on (three flip puzzles on a real board) and builds more cleanly from discovery to the ribbon-flip proof, while X offers the cube-stack view and a bigger counting generalization but orders parity before the tools for it.

overall.reason: The two packets are mathematically sound and closely parallel in grades 2-5, where Y is slightly better on concreteness, sequencing and recording space. Y is clearly better for K-1 (a strategy game and finding all tilings, against X's routine counting). Y also follows the organizer's page format throughout, while X puts Name fields on every page and lacks the required header, footer and shared rules.
